svg.title: Forward mapping leaves holes; inverse mapping does not
svg.desc: An animated flow diagram showing forward mapping pushing input pixels to the output and leaving 22 of 81 output pixels never written, then inverse mapping walking each output pixel backward through the inverse matrix to a position between input pixels, and taking either the nearest pixel or a weighted blend of the four around it.
svg.text: Which loop you write decides whether the picture has holes in it.
The same 30 degree rotation of the same 9 by 9 picture, done both ways. Every number below was measured, not illustrated.
1. Forward mapping — walk the INPUT and push each pixel to where it lands
for each input pixel: out[ floor(M · centre) ] = in[y][x]
It reads like the definition of the transformation. That is exactly why it is tempting.
INPUT — 81 pixels, every one of them read
the test pattern: a capital F
each pixel flies to
wherever it lands
OUTPUT — and 22 of the 81 were never written
amber = a hole: no input pixel ever reached it
output pixels never
assigned — 27 per cent
Look WHERE.
Not only at the edges.
Single pixels punched
through solid ink.
det(M) = 1, so the
rotation lost no area.
The rounding did.
Enlarging makes it a counting argument rather than a rounding one: 81 input pixels cannot fill 324 output pixels,
so doubling by forward mapping leaves at least 243 holes. Measured: exactly 243.
2. Inverse mapping — walk the OUTPUT and ask each pixel where it came from
for each output pixel: out[y][x] = in[ floor(M⁻¹ · centre) ]
INPUT, zoomed: columns 0 to 3, rows 1 to 4
OUTPUT — every pixel assigned
grey = clipped: 12 pixels whose source
lies outside the picture. Not holes.
Take output pixel (row 1, column 2).
its centre = (2.5, 2.5)
Send that centre BACKWARD:
It landed between pixels.
It almost always does. That is not a
failure — it is the normal case, and it is
the question interpolation answers.
Every output pixel is visited exactly once,
so holes are impossible by construction.
blue dots = the four pixel CENTRES around the landing
green dot = (1.2679, 2.9019), where the sample fell
3. Two honest answers to "the sample fell between pixels"
NEAREST NEIGHBOUR — take the pixel it fell inside
Hard edges, stair-stepped diagonals, and every value in
the output was already in the input. Nothing invented.
BILINEAR — blend the four, weighted by nearness
Smooth edges — and a value that was never in the input.
The four weights sum to exactly 1, so it cannot brighten or darken.
